pages.text: On Saturday mornings, Nana Ama’s kitchen smelled of roasting groundnuts. Efua stood beside her grandmother, stirring the bubbling sugar and watching the nuts turn golden. ‘Quick hands and patient eyes,’ said Nana Ama. ‘That is the whole secret.’
sentences: On Saturday mornings, Nana Ama’s kitchen smelled of roasting groundnuts.
Efua stood beside her grandmother, stirring the bubbling sugar and watching the nuts turn golden.
‘Quick hands and patient eyes,’ said Nana Ama.
‘That is the whole secret.’
pages.alt: A thirteen-year-old girl stirs a pot beside her grandmother in a warm kitchen, golden groundnuts and sugar glowing in the pot.

pages.text: Efua had a plan. If she learned the recipe, she could sell groundnut cakes at the school gate after lessons and earn enough to buy her own exercise books and pens. ‘A plan is only a wish until you do the sums,’ said Nana Ama, smiling. ‘Go and count.’
sentences: Efua had a plan.
If she learned the recipe, she could sell groundnut cakes at the school gate after lessons and earn enough to buy her own exercise books and pens.
‘A plan is only a wish until you do the sums,’ said Nana Ama, smiling.
‘Go and count.’
pages.alt: Efua holds a wooden spoon and looks hopefully at her grandmother, who points playfully towards an exercise book on the table.

pages.text: That night, Efua did the arithmetic in her exercise book. The ingredients for twenty packs cost twelve cedis. If she sold each pack for one cedi, she would make eight cedis profit. ‘Eight cedis a day,’ she whispered. ‘Over five school days, that is forty cedis a week.’
sentences: That night, Efua did the arithmetic in her exercise book.
The ingredients for twenty packs cost twelve cedis.
If she sold each pack for one cedi, she would make eight cedis profit.
‘Eight cedis a day,’ she whispered.
‘Over five school days, that is forty cedis a week.’
pages.alt: Efua writes costs and profit in an exercise book under a lamp, concentrating.

pages.text: On Monday she sold fourteen packs, and six were left over. On Tuesday she sold sixteen. People said the cakes were crunchy, fresh and not too sweet. But by Wednesday, the leftover cakes had gone a little soft in the damp air.
sentences: On Monday she sold fourteen packs, and six were left over.
On Tuesday she sold sixteen.
People said the cakes were crunchy, fresh and not too sweet.
But by Wednesday, the leftover cakes had gone a little soft in the damp air.
pages.alt: Efua at the school gate hands a small pack to a student; a bag of leftover packs sits at her feet.

pages.text: On Wednesday, Kwabena pulled her aside near the school gate. He glanced at the soft cakes in her bag. ‘You are wasting money,’ he said. ‘Use fewer groundnuts and a bit more sugar. Nobody will notice.’
sentences: On Wednesday, Kwabena pulled her aside near the school gate.
He glanced at the soft cakes in her bag.
‘You are wasting money,’ he said.
‘Use fewer groundnuts and a bit more sugar.
Nobody will notice.’
pages.alt: Kwabena leans in towards Efua near the school gate, speaking quietly while she looks uncertain.

pages.text: ‘And those old packs?’ said Kwabena. ‘Tell people they are fresh today. Do all this and you will make twice the profit.’ He smiled as if it were the most sensible idea in the world, and Efua did not know what to say.
sentences: ‘And those old packs?’ said Kwabena.
‘Tell people they are fresh today.
Do all this and you will make twice the profit.’ He smiled as if it were the most sensible idea in the world, and Efua did not know what to say.
pages.alt: Kwabena smiles confidently, pointing at the bag of old packs; Efua hesitates, biting her lip.

pages.text: Efua did the sums again that night, by the light of a small lamp. With fewer groundnuts, twenty packs would cost nine cedis, so she would make eleven cedis profit. That was not twice as much, as Kwabena had promised. It was only three cedis more. Still, he was right about one thing: she could make more. But she kept thinking about her customers. They trusted her, and trust, she realised, was worth more than three cedis a day.
sentences: Efua did the sums again that night, by the light of a small lamp.
With fewer groundnuts, twenty packs would cost nine cedis, so she would make eleven cedis profit.
That was not twice as much, as Kwabena had promised.
It was only three cedis more.
Still, he was right about one thing: she could make more.
But she kept thinking about her customers.
They trusted her, and trust, she realised, was worth more than three cedis a day.
pages.alt: Efua sits alone by lamplight with her exercise book, thinking hard; a window shows the night sky.

pages.text: The next morning, Efua visited Auntie Dede, who sold vegetables at the market. ‘Customers are like a garden,’ said Auntie Dede, arranging her tomatoes. ‘Treat them well and they return all year. Cheat them once and they will remember it forever.’
sentences: The next morning, Efua visited Auntie Dede, who sold vegetables at the market.
‘Customers are like a garden,’ said Auntie Dede, arranging her tomatoes.
‘Treat them well and they return all year.
Cheat them once and they will remember it forever.’
pages.alt: A kind market trader arranges tomatoes at her stall and speaks to Efua, who listens carefully.

pages.text: Efua kept her recipe honest. She even added a few extra groundnuts to every pack, which raised her cost to thirteen cedis for twenty. She wrote the day each batch was made on a small label. And she put the leftover cakes in a separate bag marked ‘Yesterday, half price’.
sentences: Efua kept her recipe honest.
She even added a few extra groundnuts to every pack, which raised her cost to thirteen cedis for twenty.
She wrote the day each batch was made on a small label.
And she put the leftover cakes in a separate bag marked ‘Yesterday, half price’.
pages.alt: Efua’s hands fill a pack with groundnut cakes and write the date on a label; a second bag is marked as half price.

pages.text: Some days, Efua made less profit. But students liked knowing exactly what they were buying, and many of them bought the half-price packs gladly. Every week, the line at the school gate grew a little longer.
sentences: Some days, Efua made less profit.
But students liked knowing exactly what they were buying, and many of them bought the half-price packs gladly.
Every week, the line at the school gate grew a little longer.
pages.alt: A longer queue of cheerful students at the school gate, Efua serving with a smile.

pages.text: One afternoon, Kwabena stood in the line like everyone else. ‘I said you were wasting money,’ he admitted. ‘But it turns out the extra groundnuts were never wasted.’ Efua smiled and held out a fresh pack. ‘That will be one cedi,’ she said.
sentences: One afternoon, Kwabena stood in the line like everyone else.
‘I said you were wasting money,’ he admitted.
‘But it turns out the extra groundnuts were never wasted.’ Efua smiled and held out a fresh pack.
‘That will be one cedi,’ she said.
pages.alt: Kwabena, at the front of the queue, sheepishly smiles as Efua holds out a pack of groundnut cakes.

pages.text: By the end of the month, Efua was selling twenty-five packs a day. She was making a little more profit than she had first planned, and her customers trusted her cakes. That night she opened her exercise book and wrote the date at the top of a new page. Then she began, carefully and honestly, to do the sums.
sentences: By the end of the month, Efua was selling twenty-five packs a day.
She was making a little more profit than she had first planned, and her customers trusted her cakes.
That night she opened her exercise book and wrote the date at the top of a new page.
Then she began, carefully and honestly, to do the sums.
pages.alt: Efua writes the date at the top of a fresh page in her exercise book, smiling quietly, a jar of groundnuts beside her.

activities.question: How much profit did Efua expect each day from twenty packs?
activities.explanation: She would take in twenty cedis and spend twelve on ingredients, so the profit is eight cedis.

activities.definition: The money left over after you pay the costs.

activities.question: Why did Efua have six packs left over on Monday?
options: She made twenty packs but sold only fourteen
She dropped six packs on the way
activities.explanation: Twenty packs minus the fourteen she sold leaves six.

activities.prompt: What do you think Efua will do? What would you do, and why?

activities.question: Kwabena promised twice the profit. What do Efua’s sums show?
options: Only three cedis more, not twice as much
activities.explanation: Eleven cedis is three more than eight. Twice eight would be sixteen. Kwabena’s claim was bigger than the truth.

activities.definition: Believing that someone is honest and will treat you fairly.

activities.question: What did Auntie Dede mean by "Customers are like a garden"?
options: Good treatment brings customers back again and again
activities.explanation: A garden grows when you look after it, and so does a business.

activities.question: Each pack with extra groundnuts costs 65 pesewas to make. What do twenty packs cost?
activities.explanation: 65 pesewas times 20 is 1,300 pesewas, which is 13 cedis (100 pesewas make one cedi).

activities.question: Why was the half-price bag an honest way to sell the leftover cakes?
options: Customers were told the truth and got a lower price
It hid that the cakes were old
It cost Efua more to make
activities.explanation: Selling old cakes at a fair lower price, clearly labelled, is honest. Calling them fresh is not.

activities.prompt: Some days Efua made less profit. Was honesty still a good business choice? Use the story to explain.
Think of a time someone pushed you to take a shortcut. What helped you decide?

items: Efua works out her costs and profit.

activities.prompt: If you sold something, what would you want your customers to say about you?
